Decimals: what does the dot mean?

Start with one ribbon and ten equal pieces. Discover tenths, hundredths and why 0.5 and 0.50 show the same amount, with a grid you can change.

One ribbon, ten equal pieces

Imagine a ribbon that is exactly one metre long. Cut it into ten equal pieces. Pick up one piece. You are holding one tenth of the original ribbon.

You can write that fraction as 1/10. You can also write it as 0.1. These are two names for the same length.

The dot is called the decimal point. Here, the zero on its left means there are no complete metres. The 1 just after the dot counts tenths of a metre.

Put five little pieces together

Line up five of your ten pieces. They reach halfway along the original ribbon.

  • As a fraction of the whole ribbon, that is 5/10.
  • As a decimal, it is 0.5.
  • In everyday words, it is one half.

Read 0.5 as “zero point five”. The point does not mean “add” or “multiply”. It separates the whole-number part from the smaller parts.

Colour a little, then a little more

The square below represents one whole. It has ten equal columns. In tenths mode, each step colours one more column.

Try colouring five columns. Then switch to hundredths without moving the slider. The coloured amount stays the same, but now you can count the tiny squares inside it.

.

Try it yourself

Make the decimal visible

A whole square has 100 small squares. Change the amount, or change how you count the pieces.

A tenth can be split again

Cut each of the ten ribbon pieces into ten smaller, equal pieces. You now have 100 tiny pieces altogether. Each is one hundredth of the original ribbon.

One hundredth is written 0.01. The first place after the point counts tenths; the second counts hundredths.

Read one place at a time
NumberWhat it means
0.1One tenth
0.01One hundredth
0.25Two tenths and five hundredths: 25 hundredths altogether

Try 25 hundredths in the activity. You have coloured one quarter of the whole square.

Why 0.5 and 0.50 match

Five columns contain fifty tiny squares. So five tenths and fifty hundredths cover the same amount. That is why 0.5 equals 0.50.

The extra zero at the end does not add any length. But its position matters: 0.05 means only five hundredths. That is much smaller than five tenths. Compare 5 and 50 in hundredths mode to see the difference.

If this feels familiar, you have already met the idea in different fractions that describe the same amount.

What if there is a whole ribbon too?

Take one complete metre of ribbon, then add three of the tenth-metre pieces. You have 1.3 metres: one whole metre and three tenths more.

For now, that is enough. Locate the point, look at each place, and think about the size of the pieces. You do not need a long calculation to understand a decimal.
